name: Jogulamba Temple, Alampur
deity: The Goddess as Jogulamba (Yogamba), with Shiva as Bala Brahmeshwara
period: An ancient Shakti Peetha beside the 7th–8th-century Navabrahma temples; present shrine rebuilt in 2005
dynasty: Badami Chalukya setting; shrine rebuilt in 2005
style: Modern reconstruction in the traditional manner, within an Early Chalukya temple precinct
summary: On the Tungabhadra at Alampur, the fierce mother Jogulamba is worshipped as one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas, her rebuilt shrine standing beside the Bala Brahma temple where her image was sheltered for six centuries.

sections.history: Alampur, on the left bank of the Tungabhadra close to its meeting with the Krishna, was long known as the western gateway of Srisailam and holds one of the finest groups of Early Chalukya temples in the Deccan. Among them the goddess Jogulamba has her seat, counted fifth among the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas in the hymn traditionally attributed to Adi Shankara. Her original shrine was destroyed in 1390, during the turbulent wars of the period, and the image was carried for safe keeping into the neighbouring Bala Brahmeshwara temple, where she was worshipped for more than six centuries. In 2005 a new temple was consecrated for her in the same precinct, restoring the goddess to a sanctum of her own beside the ancient Navabrahma shrines.
sections.architecture: The present temple, built in 2005 in the traditional manner, stands in the south-east of the Alampur precinct within sight of the Tungabhadra and the seventh- and eighth-century Navabrahma temples with their curving northern-style towers. Within, the goddess is seated on a corpse — the inert form of Shiva without Shakti — her abundant hair adorned with a scorpion, a lizard and a skull, an iconography that marks her as a fierce, protective mother. The neighbouring Bala Brahmeshwara temple, where she long resided, remains an essential part of the pilgrimage.
sections.legends: Like every Shakti Peetha, Alampur is bound to the story of Sati, who gave up her life at Daksha's sacrifice; as the grieving Shiva carried her body across the world, its parts fell to earth, and tradition holds that her upper teeth fell here. The name Jogulamba is explained locally as Yogulamba or Yogamba, the mother of yogis. Her fierce form is understood as the power that guards the household and the land, and she is worshipped together with Shiva as Bala Brahmeshwara, her consort in this sacred place.
sections.festivals: Dasara and the nine nights of Navaratri are the goddess's great festival, and Maha Shivaratri is celebrated with Bala Brahmeshwara. The temple also holds an annual Brahmotsavam, and Fridays and full-moon days draw many devotees from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: A visit to Jogulamba is naturally joined with the Navabrahma temples that surround her: pilgrims worship the goddess, then Bala Brahmeshwara, and walk among the sandstone shrines and the site museum by the river. The precinct is spacious and calm, with the Tungabhadra running beside it. The Papanasi temples and the Sangameshwara temple relocated from the river confluence lie a short drive away.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan and a midday closure; Navaratri, Fridays and full-moon days are busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. As a living Shakti shrine, respectful conduct in the goddess's presence is asked of all visitors.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance. The surrounding ASI monuments have their own rules.
visit.gettingThere: Alampur is in Jogulamba Gadwal district, about 25 km from Kurnool and some 220 km south of Hyderabad, just off the Hyderabad–Bengaluru highway (NH 44). Alampur Road railway station, on the Hyderabad–Kurnool line, is about 9 km away, with local transport to the temple.
